column2: Overcome by grief and craving, bewildered and senseless, I now, O god, in distress, have come to you for refuge.
Save me, O Krishna, sorrowful and sunk in the ocean of worldly existence; show compassion, O lord of the world, if you regard me as your devotee.
Apart from you I have no kinsman who will care for me; having found you as my lord, O god, I have no fear anywhere,
in life or in death, in acquiring or keeping, O Lord. But those vilest of men who do not duly worship you, O god —
how can there be a good destiny for them, bound by worldly existence? What use to them is family, character, learning or life,
if devotion does not arise in them for Keshava, the sustainer of the world? Those who, having taken on a demonic nature, revile you in delusion,
fall into terrible hell, born again and again; there is no deliverance for them from that ocean of hell —
those evil, vile men who defame you, O god. Wherever I may be born through the bondage of my karma,
there, O Hari, may my devotion to you always be firm. Having worshipped you, gods, Daityas, men and others who are self-controlled
have attained the supreme perfection — who would not worship you, O god? Brahma and the gods cannot praise you, O Hari;
how can I, with a human mind, praise you who are beyond Prakriti? You have been praised by me in ignorance, O Lord;
so forgive my offence, if you have compassion for me; the good forgive even one who has offended, O Hari.
Therefore be gracious, O lord of the gods, resting in your love for devotees. Whatever praise I have offered you, O god, with a devoted heart, may it all be complete — salutation to you, Vasudeva.
Praised thus by him, the Garuda-bannered god, pleased, granted him, O best of sages, all that his mind desired.
The wise man who worships the lord of the world and praises him daily with this hymn surely attains liberation.
The learned man who, pure, recites this excellent hymn at the three junctions of the day obtains dharma, wealth, desire and liberation.
Whoever reads it, hears it or recites it to others with a composed mind goes, his impurities shaken off, to the eternal world of Vishnu.
This is blessed, removes sin, grants enjoyment and liberation, and is auspicious; it is secret, very rare and holy, and should not be given to just anyone —
not to an atheist, a fool, an ungrateful or proud man, not to the evil-minded, and never to one without devotion.
It should be given to one filled with devotion, endowed with virtue and good character, a devotee of Vishnu, tranquil, and rich in faith and practice.
This excellent hymn to Purushottama, called Karunya, which I have told, is the cause of the destruction of all sins, grants happiness and liberation, and yields the fruit of every wish.
Those pure ones who always meditate on Murari, that very subtle, ancient Person, become partakers of liberation and enter Vishnu, as ghee offered with mantras enters the sacrificial fire.

He alone is the god who destroys the sorrow of existence, higher than the highest; there is nothing other than him. He is the seer, the protector and the destroyer — Vishnu, the essence of all that exists.
What use is learning, or their own virtues, sacrifices, gifts and fierce austerities, for those who have no devotion here to Krishna, the teacher of the world, giver of the bliss of liberation?

In the world he is blessed, he is pure, he is learned, he is foremost in sacrifices, austerities and virtues; he is the knower, the giver, the speaker of truth — he who has devotion to the one called Purushottama.
Having seen it and reflected with it, then, O king, by that sight make that divine image; cast off your bewildering anxiety.
Having said this, the illustrious Hari vanished; and he, having seen the dream, was filled with great wonder.
He stayed awake through that night, his mind absorbed in him, reciting the mantras of Vishnu and the hymn whose essence is him.
When the night had passed he rose, thinking of nothing else, and bathed properly in the ocean according to rule.
Having given gifts to brahmins, villages and towns, and performed his morning rites, that best of kings went forth.
With no horse, no foot soldier, no elephant and no charioteer, the king entered the great shore alone.
He saw that great tree, radiant, a mighty tree, very tall and high, holy and vast,
of great height and huge body, lying near the water, of deep madder colour, without name or species.
Then, O brahmins, the lord of men, seeing the tree, joyfully struck it with a sharp and strong axe.
The friend of Indra was about to split it in two; as he examined the wood, a wondrous sight appeared.
Vishvakarman and Vishnu, both in the form of brahmins, the illustrious pair, came then, looking like brahmins of equal age,
blazing with their own splendour, wearing divine garlands and unguents. Then they approached the king, the friend of Indra,
and said: "Great king, what are you going to do here? Why, O mighty-armed one, has this tree been felled?
Alone, in a very difficult, deserted, dense forest on the shore of the great ocean — how has this tree been felled?"
Hearing their words, O brahmins, the king, joyful, spoke to them gentle and sweet words.
Seeing those two brahmins there, like the moon and sun come down, he bowed to the two lords of the world and stood with downcast face.

I intend to make an image in order to worship the god of gods, without beginning or end, endless, lord of the worlds.
brahmapuran:50:32	I was instructed by that supreme great-souled god of gods at the end of a dream; I have told you this.
Hearing the words of the king, who resembled the lord of the gods, the lord of the universe laughed and, pleased, said to him:

Well done, well done, O king, that yours is this excellent intention. In the terrible ocean of worldly existence, like a plantain leaf,
brahmapuran:50:35	without substance, full of sorrow, crowded with desire and anger, muddy with the whirlpools of the senses, hard to cross and hair-raising,
brahmapuran:50:36	with whirlpools of hundreds of diseases, like a bubble of water — since your mind has turned to the worship of Vishnu,
brahmapuran:50:37	blessed are you, O tiger among kings, adorned with all virtues; blessed is the earth with its people, mountains, woods and forests,
brahmapuran:50:38	with its cities, villages and towns, adorned with the four classes, where you, O tiger among kings, are the lord protecting the people.
brahmapuran:50:39	Come, come, O illustrious one, and stay with us under this pleasantly cool tree, engaged in talk about dharma.
brahmapuran:50:40	This helper of mine has come, the best of craftsmen, equal to Vishvakarman himself, skilled in every work; he will make the image I describe. Leave the shore.
Hearing these words of the brahmin, the king left the ocean's shore and went near him,
and that best of kings stood in the very cool shade of the tree. Then the soul of the universe, in the form of a brahmin, gave the command
to the chief of craftsmen, O best of brahmins: "Make the images: the form of Krishna, supreme and tranquil, with eyes long as lotus petals,
bearing the Shrivatsa and Kaustubha, holding conch, discus and mace; the second, fair-limbed, white as milk, marked with the svastika,
the god bearing the plough-weapon, the mighty one called Ananta — by gods, Danavas, Gandharvas, Yakshas, Vidyadharas and serpents
his end is not known, hence he is remembered as Ananta; and the sister of Vasudeva, golden in colour and very beautiful,
the third, Subhadra, marked with every good sign."
Hearing his words, Vishvakarman, the doer of good work, made the images with auspicious marks in that very instant:
the first, of white colour, radiant like the autumn moon, with red eyes and huge body, his head fearsome with a hood,
wearing blue garments, fierce, Bala, proud of his strength, wearing a single earring, divine, bearing mace and pestle;
the second, lotus-eyed, like a dark cloud, like the atasi flower, with eyes long as lotus petals,
clad in yellow, very fierce, auspicious, marked with the Shrivatsa, his hand full with the discus, divine, Hari who removes all sins;
the third, golden in colour, with eyes long as lotus petals, clothed in variegated garments, adorned with necklace and armlets,
endowed with variegated ornaments, hung with jewelled necklaces, with full, raised breasts, lovely — so Vishvakarman fashioned them.
The king, seeing the wonder — made in a single moment, covered with pairs of divine garments, adorned with various jewels,
endowed with every good mark, very charming images — was filled with supreme wonder and said these words:

Are you two gods who have come in the guise of brahmins? Both of you are doers of wondrous deeds, of divine conduct, superhuman.
brahmapuran:50:58	Are you gods or men, Yakshas or Vidyadharas? Are you Brahma and Hrishikesha, or Vasus, or the Ashvins?
brahmapuran:50:59	I do not know your true nature, for you stand in illusory forms. I have come to you for refuge; let your true self be revealed to me.

I myself am Brahma, I am Vishnu and I am Shiva; I am Indra, king of the gods, and Yama, the restrainer of the world;
brahmapuran:51:5	the elements beginning with earth, the three sacred fires, the eater of oblations, O king; I am Varuna, lord of waters, the earth and the mountain.
brahmapuran:51:6	Whatever in the world consists of speech, the world of unmoving and moving, all that moves and does not move — there is nothing other than me.
brahmapuran:51:7	I am pleased with you, O best of kings; choose a boon, O one of good vows. I will grant whatever you desire, whatever is settled in your heart.
brahmapuran:51:8	The sight of me does not come to those without merit even in a dream; but you, through your firm devotion, have seen me face to face.
Hearing these words of Vasudeva, O brahmins, the king, his body thrilling with joy, sang this hymn:

Beloved of Shri, salutation to you; lord of Shri, clad in yellow; giver of Shri, master of Shri, abode of Shri — salutation to you, dwelling of Shri.
brahmapuran:51:11	I bow to the primal Person, the ruler, lord of all, facing every way, partless, the supreme, eternal god,
brahmapuran:51:12	beyond sound, beyond qualities, free of being and non-being, untainted, without qualities, subtle, all-knowing, sustainer of all,
brahmapuran:51:13	like a rain-cloud, devoted to the welfare of cows and brahmins, protector of all, all-pervading, sustainer of all beings.
brahmapuran:51:14	I bow to the god bearing conch and discus, mace and pestle, the boon-giving god with the lustre of a blue lotus petal.
brahmapuran:51:15	I bow to Hrishikesha, lying on the serpent couch in the milk ocean, Hari who removes all sins.
brahmapuran:51:16	Again I bow to you, lord of the gods, boon-giving and all-pervading, lord of all worlds, Vishnu, imperishable cause of liberation.
Having thus praised that god and bowed with joined palms, he prostrated himself on the ground and, bowing, said:

If you are pleased with me, O Lord, I choose the highest boon. Gods, Asuras, Gandharvas, Yakshas, Rakshasas, great serpents,
brahmapuran:51:19	Siddhas, Vidyadharas, Sadhyas, Kinnaras and Guhyakas, and the illustrious sages learned in various scriptures,
brahmapuran:51:20	wandering ascetics devoted to yoga, those who reflect on the meaning of the Veda's truth, and others who know the path of liberation meditate on the supreme state —
brahmapuran:51:21	that state, without qualities, pure and tranquil, which the wise behold — I wish to reach it by your grace, though it is very hard to attain.

May all be well with you; may you obtain everything you desire. It will be as you wish by my grace; there is no doubt.
brahmapuran:51:23	For ten thousand nine hundred years, O best of kings, rule your great kingdom without interruption.
brahmapuran:51:24	You will go to the divine state, hard for gods and Asuras to reach, where every wish is fulfilled — tranquil, secret, unmanifest and imperishable,
brahmapuran:51:25	higher than the highest, subtle, untainted, partless and fixed, free from anxiety and grief, devoid of action and cause.
brahmapuran:51:26	I will show you that supreme state called the knowable; attaining it you will reach supreme bliss and the highest goal.
brahmapuran:51:27	And your fame, O king of kings, will last here on earth as long as there are clouds and sky, as long as moon, sun and stars,
brahmapuran:51:28	as long as the seven oceans and the mountains beginning with Meru remain and the gods dwell in heaven — so long, everywhere, imperishable.
brahmapuran:51:29	The holy place named Indradyumna Lake, born from the parts of the sacrifice — bathing there even once, people attain the world of Shakra.
brahmapuran:51:30	Whoever has rice-balls offered on the bank of this auspicious lake will raise twenty-one generations of his family and go to the world of Shakra,
brahmapuran:51:31	honoured by Apsarases and by Gandharvas with the sound of song, dwelling there in a celestial car for the reigns of fourteen Indras.
brahmapuran:51:32	In the southern part of the lake, toward the south-west, stands a banyan, and near it a pavilion,
brahmapuran:51:33	covered with ketaki groves and full of various trees, with countless coconuts, champakas surrounded by bakulas,
brahmapuran:51:34	ashokas, karnikaras, punnagas, nagakesaras, patalas, amratakas, saralas, sandal and devadarus,
brahmapuran:51:35	banyans, ashvatthas, khadiras, parijatas and arjunas, hintalas, palmyras, shimshapas and badaras,
brahmapuran:51:36	karanjas, lakuchas, plakshas, jackfruits, bilvas and dhatukas, beautified and adorned with other trees of many kinds.
brahmapuran:51:37	In the bright fortnight of Ashadha, on the fifth day, under the asterism of the ancestors, they will bring us there and for seven days
brahmapuran:51:38	will install us in the pavilion with beautiful courtesans, charming with dance and song and rich in special entertainments.
brahmapuran:51:39	Fanning us with chowries with golden handles and fans adorned with jewels, auspicious women will install us.
brahmapuran:51:40	Celibate students, ascetics, graduates, the best of brahmins, forest-dwellers, householders, Siddhas and other brahmins,
brahmapuran:51:41	with hymns of various words and letters, and the sounds of Rig, Yajus and Saman, will praise Rama and Keshava again, O king.
brahmapuran:51:42	Then, having praised, seen and bowed with devotion, a man will dwell for ten thousand divine years in the glorious city of Hari,
brahmapuran:51:43	honoured by Apsarases and by Gandharvas with the sound of song; as Hari's attendant he sports there with Keshava,
brahmapuran:51:44	in a celestial car coloured like the sun, shining with jewelled necklaces, with all desires and great enjoyments he stays in the best of worlds.
brahmapuran:51:45	When his austerity is exhausted, coming here, he becomes a brahmin, lord of crores of wealth, glorious, surely a knower of the four Vedas.
Having thus given him the boon and made the covenant, Hari vanished, O brahmins, together with Vishvakarman.
The king, then delighted, his hair standing on end, felt that he had fulfilled his purpose through the sight of Hari.
Then Krishna, Rama and Subhadra, the giver of boons, on chariots like celestial cars, painted with gems and gold,
the wise king, with his ministers and family priest, had carried there with the sounds of great auspicious music,
with the sounds of various instruments and auspicious Vedic recitation, and placed them in an auspicious, holy, very charming spot.
Then, at an auspicious time, on an auspicious day under a constellation of good omen, at a favourable moment, he had the consecration performed with the brahmins,
by the prescribed method and the rites seen in the injunctions; the king, having done everything with the approval of the preceptor,
then gave the preceptor the fee according to rule, and gave wealth to the officiating priests and to others as prescribed.
Having duly performed the consecration in the temple, the best of dwellings, he installed them all by the rites seen in the injunctions.
Then, having worshipped duly with various fragrant flowers, with gold, gems, pearls and beautiful garments of many kinds,
with various divine jewels, seats, villages and towns, he gave other territories, cities and towns as well.
Having thus given in many ways, ruled the kingdom fittingly, performed various sacrifices and given many gifts,
the king, his purpose fulfilled, having given up all possessions, went to the supreme abode, the supreme state of Vishnu.
Thus, O best of sages, I have told you of the best of kings and the greatness of the region. What else do you wish to hear?
Hearing these words of Brahma, born of the unmanifest, the brahmins considered it a wonder and joyfully asked again:

At what time, O best of gods, should one go to Purushottama? By what rite should the Panchatirtha be performed, O Lord?
brahmapuran:51:62	Tell us everything separately — the fruit of bathing and giving at each holy place and of seeing the deities.

One who, fasting, stands on one foot and practises austerity at Kurukshetra for seventy thousand years, with senses and anger conquered,
brahmapuran:51:64	obtains a far greater fruit by always seeing Purushottama on the bright twelfth of Jyeshtha after fasting.
brahmapuran:51:65	Therefore in Jyeshtha, O best of sages, Purushottama should be seen with effort by the well-disciplined brahmins and others who desire heaven.
brahmapuran:51:66	Having duly performed the Panchatirtha in Jyeshtha, the best of men should see Purushottama on the twelfth of the bright fortnight.
brahmapuran:51:67	Those who see the imperishable god Purushottama on the twelfth reach Vishnu's world and never fall from it.
brahmapuran:51:68	Therefore, O best of brahmins, one should go with effort in Jyeshtha; having performed the Panchatirtha there, Purushottama should be seen.
brahmapuran:51:69	Even one who lives very far away and, pure in heart, praises Purushottama with devotion day after day, goes to Vishnu's city.
brahmapuran:51:70	The man who makes the pilgrimage to Krishna with faith and composure is freed from all sins and goes to Vishnu's world.
brahmapuran:51:71	Seeing from afar Hari's discus standing on top of the temple, and bowing to it with devotion, a man is at once freed from sin.
Then, O brahmins, the Samvartaka fire together with the wind entered the whole world, lit by the suns.
Afterwards, piercing the earth and entering Rasatala, it creates great fear for gods, Danavas and Yakshas.
Burning the world of the Nagas and whatever is on the earth here and below, O tigers among sages, it destroys everything in a moment.
Then for thousands and hundreds of twenty yojanas the swift wind and that Samvartaka fire burn all.
Then, blazing, that lord burns the entire world with its gods, Asuras and Gandharvas, Yakshas, serpents and Rakshasas.
That very fierce blazing one is known as the fire of the kalpa, with great flames, great rays and a great roaring blaze,
like a crore of suns, blazing with its splendour, it quickly burned the three worlds with gods, Asuras and men.
In such a very terrible, dreadful great dissolution, a sage of supreme righteousness was absorbed in the yoga of meditation.
He remained alone, O brahmins, famed as Markandeya; bound by the fetters of delusion, his senses tormented by hunger and thirst,
seeing that great fire, his throat, lips and palate dry, tormented by thirst and stumbling, he was then overcome with fear, O brahmins.
He wandered over the whole earth, bewildered and senseless; finding no protector, he ran here and there.
He found no place of rest where he might repose, O brahmins. "What shall I do? I do not know in whom to take refuge.
How may I see that god, the eternal lord of persons?" — thus reflecting with a single mind on the eternal god,
he reached that divine place, the cause of the great dissolution, the eternal king of banyans, famed as Purushesha.
The sage hastened to the banyan; reaching it, O best of sages, he entered at its root.
There was no fear of the fire of doom, no rain of embers, no coming of the Samvartaka, nor thunderbolt.
Their bodies wrapped in garlands of lightning, great clouds arose, terrible in form, mighty, resounding with dreadful roars.
Then all the clouds covered the vault of the sky; by them this whole earth with its mountains, forests and mines,
and all the directions, were filled and flooded with masses of water. Then those terrible clouds, O best of sages,
impelled by the Supreme One, flooded everything with water, raining great waters and filling the earth,
and they destroyed the very terrible, inauspicious, fierce fire. Then for twelve years the clouds, in the deluge,
filled everything with torrents, impelled by the great soul. Then the oceans overflowed their shores, O brahmins;
the mountains crumbled and the earth sank in the waters. On all sides those clouds, greatly whirling, the vault of the sky
having covered, perished, struck by the force of the wind. Then that terrible wind, O best of sages, Vishnu,
the god who dwells in the primal lotus, drinks up and sleeps, O brahmins. In that terrible single ocean, when moving and unmoving had perished,
when gods, Asuras and men had perished and there were no Yakshas or Rakshasas, then the sage, resting and meditating on Purushottama,
opened his eyes and saw the earth full of water; he did not see that banyan, nor the earth, nor the directions, nor the sun,
nor moon, sun, fire and wind, nor gods, Asuras and serpents. In that terrible single ocean, dark and without support,
sinking, O brahmins, he began to swim; the distressed sage wandered, floating here and there.
He sank, O brahmins, finding no protector. Seeing him thus distressed, Purushottama, pleased by his meditation, spoke to him out of compassion, O tigers among sages:

Child, you are weary; you are a boy, my devotee of good vows. Come, come quickly to me, Markandeya.
brahmapuran:53:20	Do not be afraid; you have come before me. O steadfast sage Markandeya, you are a child, oppressed with fatigue.
Hearing those words, the sage became exceedingly angry; he spoke then, O brahmins, and was repeatedly astonished:

Who is this who calls me by name, as if slighting my austerity, as if insulting my body that has lived many thousands of years?
brahmapuran:53:23	Such conduct is not practised even among the gods; Brahma, the lord of the gods, calls me 'the long-lived one.'
brahmapuran:53:24	Who, careless of his life, addressing me — whose austerity is terrible — as 'Markandeya,' wishes here to meet his death at my hands?
Having said this, O brahmins, the sage became anxious: "Is this a dream I have seen, or has this delusion come upon me?"
As he reflected thus, a thought arose that removes sorrow: "I will go for refuge with devotion to the god Purushottama."
Taking refuge in the god, his mind absorbed in him, the sage again saw that vast banyan above the water.
On a broad branch of it was a very wonderful golden, lovely divine couch fashioned by Vishvakarman,
made of diamonds and beryl, beautiful with gems and coral, set with rubies and other jewels,
covered with various spreads, adorned with various gems, filled with various wonders and adorned with a halo of light.
On it was the god Krishna in the form of a child, radiant like a crore of suns, blazing and lustrous,
four-armed, beautiful in limb, with eyes long as lotus petals, the Shrivatsa on his chest, bearing conch, discus and mace,
his chest covered with the forest garland, wearing divine earrings, his neck laden with necklaces and adorned with divine jewels.
Seeing the god, the sage, his eyes wide with wonder and his body thrilling, bowed to the god and said this:
Ah! In this terrible single ocean, when all moving and unmoving has perished, how does this one child stay here so fearless?
Though the great sage knew past, present and future, he did not then recognise the god, bewildered by his maya. When he did not recognise him, he spoke in distress:

Vain is the power of my austerity, vain my knowledge, vain my rites, vain my long life and vain my humanity,
brahmapuran:53:38	since I do not know the divine child sleeping on the couch.
Reflecting thus, floating and senseless, distressed and seeking protection, the brahmin fell into despair.
Then, O brahmins, he could not look at him, standing in his own greatness, like the morning sun, made of all splendour.
Seeing the sage approaching, the child, as if laughing, spoke then with a voice like the rumble of clouds, O tigers among sages:
Child, I know you are weary and have come to me for protection. Enter my body quickly; rest has been ordained for you by me.
Hearing his words, the bewildered sage said nothing and, helpless, entered his open mouth.
Be gracious, beloved of Kamala; be gracious, lord of the thirty gods; be gracious, slayer of Kamsa and Keshin; be gracious, destroyer of Arishta.
Be gracious, Krishna, slayer of Daityas; be gracious, ender of the Danavas; be gracious, dweller in Mathura; be gracious, joy of the Yadus.
Be gracious, younger brother of Shakra; be gracious, imperishable giver of boons. You are earth, you are water, O god, you are fire, you are wind,
you are space and you are mind, you are egoity; you are intellect and Prakriti, and the qualities beginning with sattva, O lord of the world.
You are the Person pervading the world, and higher than the Person; you are all the senses and their objects beginning with sound, O Lord.
You are the guardians of the directions and the dharmas, the Vedas and sacrifices with their fees; you are Indra, you are the god Shiva, you are the oblation and the fire.
You are Yama, king of the ancestors, O god; you yourself are the lord of the Rakshasas; you are Varuna, lord of waters; you are Vayu and the lord of wealth.
You are Ishana, you are Ananta, you are Ganesha and the six-faced one; you are the Vasus, the Rudras, the Adityas and the sky-rovers.
You are the Danavas and Yakshas, the Daityas with the hosts of Maruts, the Siddhas, Apsarases, Nagas, Gandharvas and Charanas.
You are the ancestors, the Valakhilyas and the lords of creatures, O Achyuta; you are the sages and the hosts of seers, the Ashvins and the night-rovers.
You are the other species too, whatever is called a living being. What need to say more? Whatever lies between Brahma and a blade of grass,
past, present and future — you are the world, moving and unmoving. Your supreme form, O god, unchanging, immovable and fixed,
even Brahma and the others do not know; how then others of little intelligence? O god, you are pure in nature, eternal, beyond Prakriti,
unmanifest, eternal, endless, all-pervading, the great Lord; you are space, supreme and tranquil, unborn, all-pervading and imperishable.
Who can praise you thus, without qualities and stainless? Whatever praise I have offered you, O god, confused and of little mind, forgive it all, O imperishable lord of the gods.

The brahmins worship me alone, constantly meditating on me. I am the Samvartaka light, I am the Samvartaka fire,
brahmapuran:56:27	I am the Samvartaka sun, I am the Samvartaka wind. These forms of stars that are seen in the vault of the sky —
brahmapuran:56:28	know them to be the pores of my skin, O best of brahmins. The oceans, mines of jewels, all in the four directions —
brahmapuran:56:29	know them to be my garment, my bed and my dwelling. Desire, anger, joy, fear and delusion —
brahmapuran:56:30	know all these to be my forms, O excellent one. That which men obtain by doing good works, O brahmin —
brahmapuran:56:31	truth, charity, fierce austerity and non-violence to all creatures — is ordained by me; they move within my body.
brahmapuran:56:32	Their understanding overpowered by me, they act, not by their own will. Studying the Veda properly and sacrificing with various rites,
brahmapuran:56:33	the twice-born, tranquil in mind and with anger conquered, attain me. I cannot be attained by men of evil deeds,
brahmapuran:56:34	overcome by greed, miserly, ignoble and undisciplined. Know me as the great fruit for men of cultivated minds,
brahmapuran:56:35	very hard to reach for the deluded who follow wrong disciplines. Whenever there is a decline of dharma, O excellent one,
brahmapuran:56:36	and a rise of adharma, then I bring myself forth. When Daityas devoted to violence, who cannot be slain by the best of gods,
brahmapuran:56:37	and fearsome Rakshasas arise in this world, then I am born in the houses of those of holy deeds;
brahmapuran:56:38	entering a human body, I pacify everything. Having created gods and men, Gandharvas, serpents and Rakshasas,
brahmapuran:56:39	and the unmoving beings, I withdraw them through my own maya; at the time of action I reflect again on the body and create.
brahmapuran:56:40	I enter a human body for the sake of binding the bounds of right order. My dharma is white in the Krita age and dark in the Treta;
brahmapuran:56:41	on reaching the Dvapara it is red, and in the Kali age black; at that time three parts are adharma.
brahmapuran:56:42	And when the time of the end arrives, becoming Time, exceedingly fierce, I alone destroy the three worlds, all that is unmoving and moving.
brahmapuran:56:43	I am of three dharmas, the soul of the universe, bringer of happiness to all worlds, undivided, all-pervading, endless, Hrishikesha, the wide-striding one.
brahmapuran:56:44	I alone turn the wheel of time; that form of Brahman is mine alone — the stilling of all beings and the effort made by all beings.
brahmapuran:56:45	Thus my self is well placed in all beings, O best of sages, O best of brahmins, yet no one knows me.
brahmapuran:56:46	In all the world my devotees worship me in every way. Whatever painful experience you have had in me, O brahmin,
brahmapuran:56:47	all of it is for the arising of your happiness and for your good, O sinless one. Whatever unmoving and moving you have seen in the world,
brahmapuran:56:48	all of it is ordained by me, the self who brings beings into existence. I am named Narayana, bearing conch, discus and mace.
brahmapuran:56:49	As long as a thousand ages revolve, O brahmin sage, so long I, the soul of the universe, sleep, bewildering all the worlds.
brahmapuran:56:50	Thus I remain here all this time, O best of sages, not a child yet in the form of a child, until Brahma awakens.
brahmapuran:56:51	And a boon was given to you by me in the form of Brahma, O best of brahmins, being pleased again and again, O one honoured by hosts of brahmin sages.
brahmapuran:56:52	Having made all one ocean, when moving and unmoving had perished, you came forth unknown to me; then the world was shown to you.
brahmapuran:56:53	When you entered the inside of my body and saw the whole world, you were astonished and did not understand.
brahmapuran:56:54	Then, O brahmin sage, you were quickly expelled by me from my mouth, and my self, hard for gods and Asuras to know, has been declared to you.
brahmapuran:56:55	Until that Lord Brahma of great austerity awakens, so long, O brahmin sage, move about here happily and without fear.
brahmapuran:56:56	Then, when that grandsire of all worlds has awakened, I alone will create beings and bodies, O best of brahmins —
brahmapuran:56:57	space, earth, light, wind and water, and whatever unmoving and moving there may be here in the world.
Having said this, O brahmins, Madhava spoke to him again when a full thousand ages had passed, with a voice deep as a cloud:

O sage, tell me truly for what purpose you praised me. Choose the best boon; I will give it without delay.
brahmapuran:56:60	You are long-lived among the gods, my devotee of firm vows; therefore, O best of brahmins, obtain long life again.
Hearing his auspicious words and looking at him again, he suddenly fell with his head to the ground, bowed and said again:

I have seen your supreme form, O lord of the gods; truly this delusion of mine has gone now that I have seen you, O Hari.
brahmapuran:56:63	This is what I wish, O Lord, by your grace, for the good of the worlds and to allay their various disputes —
brahmapuran:56:64	a refutation of the arguments of the Shaivas and Bhagavatas: in this excellent, holy, pure region of Purushottama
brahmapuran:56:65	I shall build a supreme and great temple of Shiva, O god, and install Shankara there in your place.
brahmapuran:56:66	Then people in this world will know that Hari and Ishvara are of one form. The lord of the world answered that great sage again:

This linga, the supreme god, cause and lord of the worlds, for worship and to allay various disputes —
brahmapuran:56:68	at my command, O best of brahmins, quickly build a temple of Shiva; by its power you will dwell imperishably in Shiva's world.
brahmapuran:56:69	When Shiva is installed, O brahmin, I shall be installed; there is no difference between us, one nature made twofold.
brahmapuran:56:70	He who is Rudra is Vishnu himself, and he who is Vishnu is Maheshvara; there is no difference between the two, as between wind and space.
brahmapuran:56:71	The deluded one does not know that he who is Garuda-bannered is himself the bull-bannered one, the three-eyed destroyer of Tripura.
brahmapuran:56:72	Therefore, O brahmin, build a temple of Shiva marked with your name, and to the north of the god of gods make a very beautiful holy place;
brahmapuran:56:73	it will be famed in the world of men as Markandeya's Pool, O best of brahmins, destroying all sins.
Having said this, O best of sages, the god, the all-pervading Janardana, vanished right there before Markandeya.
Bowing to Vainateya standing before Krishna, one is freed from all sins and then goes to Vishnu's city.
Whoever, having seen the banyan and Vainateya, sees Purushottama, Sankarshana and Subhadra, goes to the supreme goal.
Entering Vishnu's temple and circumambulating it three times, one should worship Sankarshana with devotion using his own mantra and propitiate him:

Salutation to you, Rama, bearer of the plough; salutation to you whose weapon is the pestle; salutation to you, beloved of Revati; salutation to you, loving to your devotees;
brahmapuran:57:23	salutation to you, best of the strong; salutation to you, upholder of the earth; enemy of Pralamba, salutation to you; protect me, elder brother of Krishna.
Having thus propitiated Ananta, the invincible, worshipped by the gods, shaped like the peak of Kailasa, with a face lovelier than the moon,
the god clad in blue, his head fearsome with hoods, the mighty plough-bearer adorned with a single earring,
the son of Rohini, a man obtains with devotion the fruit he desires; freed from all sins, he goes to Vishnu's world.
Having enjoyed happiness there until the dissolution of beings, when his merit is exhausted the man comes here and, in an excellent family of yogins,
becoming the foremost of brahmins, master of the meaning of all scriptures, he attains knowledge there and reaches rare liberation.
Having thus worshipped the plough-bearer, the wise one, well composed, should then worship Krishna with the twelve-syllable mantra.
The steadfast who always worship Purushottama with devotion using the twelve-syllable mantra surely attain liberation.
Neither gods, nor yogins, nor Soma-drinkers reach the goal that those devoted to the twelve-syllable mantra reach, O brahmins.
Therefore, having worshipped Krishna, teacher of the world, with devotion using that very mantra, with perfumes, flowers and the like, one should bow and propitiate him:
Having thus propitiated the lord of gods, giver of boons, loving to his devotees, the god who removes all sins and grants the fruit of every desire,
Krishna with stout shoulders, two-armed, with eyes long as lotus petals, broad-chested, mighty-armed, clad in yellow, with a lovely face,
holding conch, discus and mace, adorned with crown and armlets, endowed with every good mark and adorned with the forest garland —
having seen him, joined his palms and prostrated like a staff, a man obtains the fruit of thousands of horse sacrifices, O brahmins.
Whatever fruit is declared for bathing and giving at all holy places, a man obtains that fruit by seeing Krishna and bowing.
Whatever fruit comes from a sacrifice with all jewels and much gold, a man obtains that fruit by seeing Krishna and bowing.
Whatever fruit is in all the Vedas and in all sacrifices, a man obtains that fruit by bowing to Krishna.
Whatever fruit comes from all gifts, vows and observances, a man obtains that fruit by seeing Krishna and bowing.
Whatever fruit is declared for various fierce austerities, a man obtains that fruit by seeing Krishna and bowing.
Whatever fruit comes from celibacy properly observed, a man obtains that fruit by seeing Krishna and bowing.
Whatever fruit belongs to a householder who follows the prescribed conduct, a man obtains that fruit by seeing Krishna and bowing.
Whatever fruit is declared for the forest-dweller's life in the woods, a man obtains that fruit by seeing Krishna and bowing.
Whatever fruit is declared for renunciation as prescribed, a man obtains that fruit by seeing Krishna and bowing.
What need to say more about his greatness, O brahmins? Seeing Krishna with devotion, a man attains rare liberation.
Freed from sins arising over crores of kalpas, pure in heart, endowed with supreme glory and all virtues,
in a radiant celestial car rich in every desire, raising twenty-one generations, a man goes to Vishnu's city.
Enjoying charming pleasures there for a hundred kalpas with Gandharvas and Apsarases, like four-armed Vishnu,
falling from there and coming here, he is born in an excellent family of brahmins, all-knowing, versed in all the Vedas and free from envy,
devoted to his own dharma, tranquil, generous and devoted to the welfare of beings; attaining the knowledge of Vishnu, he then attains liberation.
Then, having worshipped Subhadra, loving to her devotees, with her mantra, one should propitiate her, O brahmins, bowing with joined palms:
Salutation to you, all-pervading Goddess; salutation to you, giver of auspicious happiness; protect me, lotus-eyed one; Katyayani, salutation to you.
Having thus propitiated that Goddess, sustainer and benefactor of the world, Subhadra, sister of Baladeva, the boon-giving auspicious one,
a man goes to Vishnu's city in a celestial car that moves at will; having sported there like a god until the dissolution of beings,
on attaining human birth here he becomes a brahmin learned in the Veda, and attaining the yoga of Hari there, he surely obtains liberation.
